Title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Early Detection of Critical Outcomes in the Emergency Department
Realism_Notes: Real MIMIC-IV-ED data (n=425,087) used but evaluation is proxy-metric only (accuracy, AUROC, AUPRC, rule fidelity/coverage/consistency) with no human participants at any stage; matches rubric's Level-1 positive example verbatim ('faithfulness metrics computed on a neural network trained on MIMIC without clinician evaluation') and the explicit miscoding warning that real clinical data alone does not elevate the level.
EV_Notes: No human participants at any stage (proxy metrics only); all four EV dimensions score at floor, consistent with the typical Realism_Level=1 profile (0/0/0-1/0).
Outcome_Claimed: "facilitating clinicians in early detection of critically ill presenting to the ED"; "interpretability through rule extraction and analysis from the GB model is explored, supporting clinical trust and informed decision-making"; "these rules offer clinicians practical and interpretable guidelines for quickly identifying high-risk patients during triage... suggest their viability for integration into existing electronic triage systems"
Outcome_Demonstrated: GB slightly outperforms LR (Accuracy 78.21% vs 77.27%, AUROC 0.887 vs 0.863, AUPRC 0.445 vs 0.370); te2rules extracted 43 rules from the GB model with overall fidelity 98.90% (positive fidelity 100%, negative fidelity 98.88%); rules further characterised by Coverage/Consistency/Relative-Coverage metrics and an aggregated Rule Coverage Index. No human comprehension, trust, or decision-quality evidence collected.
QR_Notes: QR1=0: paper makes clinical deployment/integration claims ("viability for integration into existing electronic triage systems", "facilitating clinicians") with zero clinician evaluation -- matches rubric boundary example verbatim. QR2=1: metrics used (fidelity/coverage) are coherent with the narrower technical RQ but the paper's clinical-utility framing outstrips what any task actually tests. QR3=2: AUROC/AUPRC/Youden's index and te2rules fidelity/coverage/consistency formulas are all formally defined with citations (Fluss et al. 2005; Lal et al. 2024; Al-A'araji et al. 2020). QR4=2: direct quantitative fidelity score (98.90%) reported between rule set and GB model. QR5=2: dataset (MIMIC-IV-ED, n=425,087, 2011-2019, Beth Israel Deaconess), model config (GB 100 trees, te2rules precision threshold 85%, 5-fold CV), and procedure fully specified.
Notes: Single domain (ED triage / EHR data via MIMIC-IV-ED), single method. te2rules performs POST-HOC rule extraction from an already-trained GB black-box model (Section II-D) -- not an inherently-interpretable model in Rudin's sense -- so #inherently_interpretable tag was withheld per xai_method_taxonomy.md guidance; flagged for reviewer. Study_Design judgment call: retrospective analysis of a large real-world cohort could also be argued as Observational, but coded MethodPaper because the paper's own framing and evaluation are limited to technical/proxy metrics with no assessment of clinical utility (README MethodPaper definition).
Method_Justification_Notes: No explicit rationale given for choosing te2rules/rule extraction over other XAI methods (e.g., SHAP, LIME); Methods section D simply states "we used the te2rules framework to extract readable rules" with no comparative justification.
Reg_Notes: All four Reg_* default to No: no comprehension test administered (rules merely presented/described by authors, not tested on clinicians); no trust-calibration evidence (no trust measure at all, let alone across varying reliability conditions); no uncertainty/failure-mode transparency surfaced to a user (data imbalance is discussed only as a study limitation, not surfaced to an end-user); no workflow-safety evidence (Realism_Level=1, EV_Environment=0, no clinical workflow context at all).

Title: Emergency Department Triage Hospitalization Prediction Based on Machine Learning and Rule Extraction
Realism_Notes: Real MIMIC-IV-ED data used for prediction modelling and rule extraction, but only proxy fidelity metrics reported; no human participants or clinical workflow context. Per rubric decision table: real clinical data + proxy metrics only + no participants = Level 1, not Level 0 (an evaluation was conducted, just not a human one).
EV_Notes: All four EV dimensions are 0: no participants, no elicited human task, no interface, only computational fidelity metrics (fidelity=0.879; positive fidelity=1; negative fidelity=0.785).
Outcome_Claimed: "The objective of this work was to investigate the usefulness of explainable AI (XAI) functionality in the ED triage hospitalization prediction modelling based on machine learning and rule extraction."; "interpretable rules were extracted with a high precision threshold, demonstrating the rules' overall accuracy in replicating the model's behaviour"; "providing ED practitioners with actionable insights."
Outcome_Demonstrated: GB model: 83% accuracy, 82% sensitivity, 84% specificity, AUROC 0.919 for hospitalization prediction (n=334,480 train / 83,620 test). TE2Rules extracted 35 rules at precision threshold 0.9; overall fidelity to the GB model = 0.879 (positive fidelity = 1.0, negative fidelity = 0.785). No clinician validation of the rules was performed; authors state this explicitly as future work.
QR_Notes: QR_Outcome: fidelity metric is a formally defined, citable measure (TE2Rules, Lal et al. arXiv:2206.14359) and AUROC/accuracy/sensitivity/specificity are standard. QR_Faithfulness=2: direct quantitative fidelity assessment (overall/positive/negative fidelity scores) satisfies the 'Direct quantitative assessment' example in the rubric. QR_Reporting=1: dataset (MIMIC-IV-ED v2.2, n, 2011-2019, train/test split) and rule-extraction procedure (TE2Rules, precision threshold 0.9) are reasonably specified, but ML model hyperparameters (tree depth, learning rate, etc.) and cross-validation procedure are not given -- typical of this 2-page conference format.
Notes: Domain = EHR (ED triage/hospitalization prediction from structured EHR features: vitals, triage acuity, meds, microbiology, prior visits -- no more specific specialty label applies). Rule extraction here is POST-HOC: TE2Rules approximates a separately-trained 100-tree GB black-box model; it is not an inherently-interpretable model in the Rudin sense (the classifier used for prediction is GB; the rule list is a global surrogate). DoshiVelez_Category and VilonLongo_Category agree (both point to no-human, proxy-only evaluation) -- no cross-check disagreement to flag. Paper explicitly frames clinician validation and cross-model benchmarking as future work, not yet done.
Method_Justification_Notes: No explicit comparative rationale is given for choosing rule extraction/TE2Rules over other XAI methods (e.g., SHAP, LIME). The paper cites a general field-level motivation for interpretability ("The support of interpretable rule functionality in this work addresses a pressing concern raised by many researchers [7]" -- citing Rudin 2019) but this is a motivation for the XAI subfield, not a stated justification for why TE2Rules specifically was selected. Coded NotReported per rubric guidance not to infer justification the paper doesn't state.
Reg_Notes: All four Reg_* columns default No: no comprehension test, no trust-calibration test (Trust_Claim=None), no uncertainty/failure-mode disclosure to any user, and no workflow evaluation (Realism_Level=1, EV_Environment=0). Paper explicitly defers clinician/expert validation to future work rather than claiming it was done.

Title: Explainable NLP Model for Predicting Patient Admissions at Emergency Department Using Triage Notes
Realism_Notes: Boundary case between Level 1 and 2. Real ED triage-note data used (not benchmark/synthetic); one physician co-author informally reviewed LIME explanations for 2 illustrative cases in the Discussion ('the evaluation was conducted in collaboration with a physician... one of the co-authors'). No structured evaluation task assigned, no independent participants, no systematic sample beyond 2 examples. Coded at the lower level (1) per rubric's ambiguous-case rule; Level 2 is a defensible alternative given the clinician involvement — flagged for reviewer.
EV_Notes: Mixed profile relative to Realism_Level=1: EV_Participant=2 (ED physician co-author reviewed explanations, but outside normal clinical workflow role and not an independent/blinded participant). EV_Task=1 (narrative face-validity commentary on 2 cherry-picked examples, not an assigned clinical decision task). EV_Environment=0 (LIME output shown as a static color-coded text figure, no interactive interface). EV_Outcome=0 (no scale, accuracy metric, or gold-standard comparison; only qualitative commentary).
Outcome_Claimed: Abstract: 'The results show that the proposed model provides satisfactory accuracy along with an interpretable understanding of the factors contributing to patient admission.' Conclusion: 'The NLP-based explanations could offer valuable insights for physicians, aiding in the understanding of the model's high or low probabilities of admission.'
Outcome_Demonstrated: Classification performance validated via 3-fold CV on ~162K triage-note records: CamemBERT AUROC=0.75, precision=0.69, recall=0.70, F1=0.70 (Table 3). Explanation quality/clinical utility itself is not formally demonstrated: only 2 illustrative LIME examples shown, discussed qualitatively by one physician co-author; no systematic sample, comparison condition, fidelity/faithfulness metric, or independent raters.
QR_Notes: QR_Participant=1: physician reviewer is ED-specialty-appropriate but is a co-author (non-independent, unblinded, n=1) reviewing only 2 cherry-picked examples, a limitation not acknowledged as such (though future 'larger study' with human-in-the-loop is proposed). QR_Task=1: face-validity commentary loosely matches the stated goal of 'exploring the explainability aspect' but is not a systematic protocol. QR_Outcome=0: no validated instrument or defined outcome measure for the explanation review. QR_Faithfulness=1: authors discuss whether LIME-highlighted words align with known clinical risk factors (face validity) with no formal fidelity/stability metric — matches rubric's 'indirect/partial assessment' example. QR_Reporting=1: model/dataset well specified (CamemBERT/FlauBERT params, embedding dim, n=162K, Amiens-Picardy 2015-2019) but LIME configuration (features/samples/kernel width) unspecified and the physician-review procedure described only in abstract terms.
Notes: Domain: ED triage-note admission prediction; coded EHR per schema_README's inclusive definition since no ED-specific domain label exists. Single XAI method (LIME), no method breakdown needed. Flags: (1) Eval_Type coded None because no minimum requirement of the 6 named types is met by the informal 2-example physician review — tension with Realism_Level=1/EV_Participant=2 which do register the clinician's informal involvement; flagged rather than silently resolved. (2) DoshiVelez_Category coded FunctionallyGrounded per the 2026-07-23 tie-break rule (Eval_Type=None, N_Participants>0) — documented, not a silent mismatch. (3) Physician evaluator is a paper co-author, not an independent recruited participant — conflict-of-interest/independence concern relevant to QR_Participant and Trust_Claim interpretation. (4) Paper states its primary focus is 'exploring the explainability aspect... rather than solely prioritizing higher performance.'
Method_Justification_Notes: Section III.D: 'LIME is model-agnostic, meaning it can be used to explain the predictions of any ML model, regardless of the type of model or algorithm used' and 'because LIME is model-agnostic, it can be used with a wide range of NLP models, including Deep Learning models like transformers.' No comparison to alternative XAI methods (e.g., SHAP, attention) is given; model-agnosticism/transformer-compatibility is the only stated rationale.
Reg_Notes: Reg_Comprehension=No: physician co-author informally commented on plausibility but was never tested for correct interpretation. Reg_TrustCalibration=No: no trust measure administered, let alone across varying model reliability (Trust_Claim=Plausibility, not Calibrated). Reg_UncertaintyTransparency=No: a raw admission probability ('64%', Fig. 2) is a model output score, not a framed uncertainty/failure-mode transparency mechanism (no OOD flag, no explicit reliability caveat). Reg_WorkflowSafety=No, consistent with Realism_Level=1 and EV_Environment=0 — no realistic workflow evaluation conducted.

Title: Deep Learning for Emergency Department Sustainability: Interpretable Prediction of Revisit
Realism_Notes: Small-scale pilot (Sec 4.6) is the highest-realism component: physicians used the SHAP-enabled bipartite interface (Fig. 3) with real KVGH patient data and gave survey feedback on clinical utility and trustworthiness. No live EHR integration and no measured clinical outcome; task was a qualitative survey, not an actual discharge decision, so coded 2 (Simulated) not 3/4. Mixed EV profile (PV=3, TV=1, EV_E=1, OV=1) matches the rubric's own worked example of a Level-2 study with PV=3 (real clinicians, artificial task/interface).
EV_Notes: Physicians are described as evaluating an ED-revisit tool at their own ED-affiliated institution -> EV_Participant=3 (clinician in role). Task was two open survey questions on clinical utility and trustworthiness, no assigned discharge decision or with/without-XAI comparison -> EV_Task=1 (artificial/rating task). The bipartite interface (Fig. 3) is a purpose-built research prototype, not the actual deployed EHR/CDSS -> EV_Environment=1. Outcome is self-reported qualitative commentary only -> EV_Outcome=1. Mixed profile (real clinicians + artificial task/interface/outcome) is itself the finding, per rubric guidance, not a coding error.
Outcome_Claimed: Abstract: In a small-scale pilot evaluation using the SHAP-enabled interface, participating physicians reported the system helped surface high-risk cohorts and reduced cognitive workload by consolidating relevant patient information for rapid cross-checking. An interpretable CNN-based clinical decision support system can predict ED revisit risk from multimodal EHR data and demonstrates practical usability in a real-world clinical setting, supporting targeted discharge planning and follow-up. Discussion (Sec 5): These insights enhance the interpretability and credibility of the model and therefore build clinician trust and support the potential integration of the model into real-world medical decision-making.
Outcome_Demonstrated: Model performance is formally demonstrated with cross-validation and an adequate sample: CNN with binary-transformed features achieved sensitivity 0.717 [0.695,0.738], accuracy 0.846 [0.842,0.850], AUROC 0.853 (8:2 split, 10-fold Monte Carlo CV, Clopper-Pearson CIs, n=184,653 ED EHR records), outperforming ML (SVM, LR, RF) and other DL (MLP, LSTM) baselines on sensitivity/AUROC (Table 7). For the XAI/interface component specifically, nothing is formally demonstrated with a validated instrument, comparison condition, or a reported/adequate sample size -- the small-scale pilot (Sec 4.6) reports only unquantified qualitative physician commentary, no stated N, no named survey instrument, and no comparison condition.
QR_Notes: QR_Participant=1: physicians from a single collaborating institution (KVGH), unspecified N, used to support the broader Abstract claim of practical usability in a real-world clinical setting without acknowledging the pilot's generalisability limits (cf. rubric example: convenience sample from a single institution with claims of broad generalisability). QR_Task=1: the 2-question survey addresses the pilot's own stated questions (utility, trust) but the Discussion/Conclusion claims of building clinician trust and supporting integration into real-world medical decision-making exceed what an uncontrolled qualitative survey can support. QR_Outcome=0: no named or validated instrument, no reliability statistic, no citation -- qualitative insights gathered informally (Sec 4.6). QR_Faithfulness=1: only face-validity commentary reported -- Physicians observed that the high importance of the Subjective feature is clinically sound (Sec 4.5) -- no fidelity/stability metric computed. QR_Reporting=1: model architecture/hyperparameters and dataset are reported in full detail (Tables 1-5, IRB KSVGH23-CT5-04), but the SHAP configuration (explainer variant, background set) and the pilot survey instrument/N/analysis method are not specified.
Notes: Domain is Emergency Department discharge/revisit prediction from EHR data; no specialty-specific controlled-vocabulary term applies, coded EHR per README guidance. Single XAI method (SHAP) used, both locally (per-prediction contribution in the interface, e.g. Subjective 85.3% for a given prediction, Sec 4.6) and globally (dataset-wide SHAP feature-importance analysis, Sec 4.5) -> XAI_Scope=Both. Eval_Type coded TrustQuestionnaire since independent physicians completed an assigned survey task, per the schema_README's HumanGrounded/TrustQuestionnaire clarification (2026-07-23) -- distinct from the Eval_Type=None+N>0 tie-break, which covers informal task-less commentary. N_Participants is never numerically reported (participating physicians, plural, no count anywhere in the text) -- flagged for human reviewer; cannot be derived from the PDF.
Method_Justification_Notes: Sec 3.6: SHAP quantifies the marginal contribution of each variable by assessing its impact across different feature subsets, thereby providing a consistent and theoretically grounded explanation of model predictions -- computational/theoretical justification (consistency, Shapley-additivity grounding). Same passage continues: such interpretability enables clinicians to understand which variables most strongly influence predictive outcomes and improves trust in automated decision support -- a cognitive/clinical-comprehension rationale. Coded Mixed with Computational as primary (the theoretical-grounding claim is the stated reason for the method choice; clinician comprehension is framed as a downstream benefit, not the selection criterion).
Reg_Notes: All four default to No -- no explicit tested evidence for any criterion. Reg_Comprehension: physicians viewed/commented on SHAP output but no comprehension check or correct-interpretation task was administered. Reg_TrustCalibration: plausibility commentary was not tested against varying model correctness (no comparison of trust when the model was right vs wrong); consistent with Trust_Claim=Plausibility, not Calibrated. Reg_UncertaintyTransparency: the interface displays SHAP contributions and raw patient data but no confidence score, OOD flag, or explicit unreliability condition is surfaced to the user; the paper's Clopper-Pearson CIs are a research-level performance statistic, not a user-facing uncertainty display. Reg_WorkflowSafety: Realism_Level=2 and EV_Environment=1, both below the Realism_Level>=3 / EV_Environment>=2 cross-check threshold in the README; no specific justification for an exception is offered in the paper.

Title: Development and Assessment of an Interpretable Machine Learning Triage Tool for Estimating Mortality After Emergency Admissions
Realism_Notes: Coded per workflow_realism_rubric.md 'Common miscodings' rule: real EHR data (SGH ED, Singapore, 2009-2016, n=323,509 admission episodes across training/validation/testing cohorts) is used, but the evaluation consists solely of computational metrics (AUC/ROC, parsimony plots) with zero human participants and no clinical workflow context tested -- 'real data alone does not elevate the level.' No clinician or clinical-proxy interaction with the SERP score or its explanation was assessed.
EV_Notes: All four EV dimensions score floor values: pure retrospective computational validation -- no participants (EV_Participant=0), no elicited human decision task (EV_Task=0), no interface presented to any user (EV_Environment=0), and the measured outcome (AUC for mortality prediction) is the underlying model's own target-variable accuracy against death-registry ground truth, not a human decision-quality or patient-outcome evaluation of using the tool (EV_Outcome=0). Consistent with the rubric's typical Realism_Level=1 profile.
Outcome_Claimed: Abstract objective: 'To develop an interpretable machine learning tool based on a parsimonious list of variables available at ED triage; provide a simple, early, and accurate estimate of patients' risk of death; and evaluate the tool's predictive accuracy compared with several established clinical scores.' Conclusion: 'SERP had better prediction performance than existing triage scores while maintaining easy implementation and ease of ascertainment in the ED. It has the potential to be widely applied and validated in different circumstances and health care settings.' Discussion frames SERP as 'simple, quick to calculate, transparent, and interpretable.'
Outcome_Demonstrated: SERP-30d achieved AUC 0.821 (95% CI, 0.796-0.847) for 2-day, 0.826 (0.811-0.841) for 7-day, 0.823 (0.814-0.832) for 30-day, and 0.810 (0.799-0.821) for inpatient mortality on a temporally distinct testing cohort (42,676 admissions from 2016), outperforming PACS, MEWS, NEWS, CART, RAPS, and REMS on the same test set with bootstrapped 95% CIs and death-registry-linked ground truth. This demonstrates superior discriminative accuracy of the underlying point-based model. No comprehension, trust, decision-quality, or workflow benefit of the tool's interpretability was tested; authors explicitly flag this as open: 'the most important unanswered question is whether SERP can improve outcomes in actual clinical practice. To address this, prospective studies are needed...'
QR_Notes: QR_Outcome=2: primary outcome (2d/7d/30d/inpatient mortality) is linked via the national death registry to deidentified EHR records -- an unambiguous, non-self-report ground truth; AUC/ROC is a formally defined, standard discrimination metric appropriately applied. QR_Faithfulness=2: SERP is an inherently interpretable additive point-based score (Rudin 2019 sense) -- Table 2 discloses the exact point value for every variable category comprising the model, i.e. the explanation IS the full model computation, not a post-hoc approximation of a separate black box; faithfulness is structural/complete by construction. QR_Reporting=2: XAI method (AutoScore, cited, eMethods/eFigure 1 protocol), underlying model (ML variable selection + logistic-regression-derived point system), dataset (n, SGH ED Singapore, 2009-2016, STROBE-guideline reporting), and evaluation procedure (train/validation/test split, bootstrapped 95% CIs, 6 comparator scores) all reported with replication-level detail.
Notes: Domain: ED triage/mortality risk prediction using structured EHR variables (vital signs, demographics, comorbidities); no secondary domain. XAI_Method note: SERP is generated via the AutoScore ML framework (variable selection + logistic regression converted to an additive point system) and functions like existing early-warning/triage scores (MEWS, NEWS, CART) -- coded RuleExtraction/inherently-interpretable per xai_method_taxonomy.md, not post-hoc explanation of a separate black-box model. DoshiVelez_Category is a mechanical function of Eval_Type=ProxyMetric + N_Participants=0, no disagreement to flag. Illustrates the RQ1 concern that 'interpretable' is often a design claim asserted from model architecture (sparsity, additivity) rather than something empirically tested with clinicians -- no comprehension check, trust measure, or decision-quality/workflow study accompanies the AUC validation.
Method_Justification_Notes: Introduction: 'In the fast-paced ED environment, a scoring tool needs to be accurate and straightforward' (workflow framing). Discussion: 'SERP is an additive, point-based triage tool, making it simple, quick to calculate, transparent, and interpretable' (cognitive/comprehensibility framing). Discussion: 'Because our SERP scores only comprise objective elements, they can be easily computed by trained medical assistants or integrated into an existing hospital EHR, without the need for professional medical personnel. Therefore, one can rapidly estimate a patient's risk of death without adversely affecting ED workloads, which is important in the fast-paced ED environment' (explicit workflow/deployment justification: low latency, non-specialist usability, EHR integration). Coded Mixed with Workflow as primary given the weight of the deployment/ED-workload argument relative to the comprehensibility framing.
Reg_Notes: Reg_Comprehension=No: no comprehension check or correct-interpretation task administered to any clinician. Reg_TrustCalibration=No: no trust measure of any kind -- Trust_Claim=None. Reg_UncertaintyTransparency=No: 95% CIs are reported for model performance in the paper but are not surfaced to an end-user as part of the tool's output; no confidence score, OOD flag, or reliability caveat accompanies the SERP score itself. Reg_WorkflowSafety=No: cross-checked against Realism_Level=1 and EV_Environment=0 -- no realistic clinical workflow evaluation was conducted; authors explicitly state prospective real-world validation is future work, not yet performed.

Title: Machine learning enables early risk stratification of hymenopteran stings: evidence from a tropical multicenter cohort
Realism_Notes: Real clinical data (942-patient Hainan multicenter cohort) but proxy-metric-only evaluation of the SHAP explanation (feature importance bar/beeswarm/heatmap/force plots plus bootstrap stability of SHAP values), no human participants evaluate the explanation at any stage -- matches workflow_realism_rubric.md decision table row 'Real clinical data, proxy metrics only, no human participants -> 1' rather than 0, since the XAI component (SHAP) is itself evaluated via a proxy stability metric, just with no clinical workflow context or human evaluator.
EV_Notes: All four EV dimensions score floor values consistent with Realism_Level=1. EV_Environment scored 0 rather than 1 despite the existence of a deployed web-based risk calculator (Figure 9): no participant is shown to interact with the tool in this study -- the two worked examples (a 38-year-old male, a 58-year-old female) are run by the authors themselves as illustrative demonstrations, not an evaluated interface session with clinician end-users.
Outcome_Claimed: Abstract/Conclusion: 'We developed and validated an interpretable machine learning model for early prediction of severe outcomes following hymenopteran stings... We developed an interpretable, deployable tool for early triage of hymenopteran sting patients in tropical settings. Emergency integration may improve clinical decisions and outcomes.' Discussion: SHAP interpretability 'offer[s] clinicians transparent insight into model rationale' and supports 'frontline clinicians in formulating dynamic intervention strategies.'
Outcome_Demonstrated: Internal retrospective validation only: Extra Trees model achieved AUC 0.959-0.982, recall 0.919-0.956, precision 0.866-0.926 on a held-out test split (30% of n=942, with only 23 high-risk cases); simplified 5-feature XGBoost model achieved AUC 0.937-0.940. SHAP (bar plot, beeswarm, heatmap, force plots) identified leukocyte count, hypotension, and creatinine as top global predictors, with bootstrap resampling showing SHAP-value coefficient of variation <15% across 100 iterations. No human comprehension, trust, decision-quality, or patient-outcome evaluation was performed. Authors explicitly caution: 'given the small number of high-risk cases, these high AUC values may overestimate real-world performance and require external validation.' No external validation was conducted.
QR_Notes: QR_Participant=0 per quality_rubric.md boundary note ('a proxy-metric study claiming this method will improve clinical decisions: QR1=0') -- paper claims the tool may 'improve clinical decisions and outcomes' and cites literature that 'interpretable AI models significantly improve clinician trust and decision-making accuracy' with zero clinician or lay participants in its own evaluation. QR_Task=1: the narrower stated Objective ('develop and validate an interpretable ML model') is well-served by the train/test/bootstrap design, but the paper's broader framing of clinical-decision improvement is not tested by any comparison task. QR_Outcome=2: AUC/recall/precision are formally defined, standard, appropriately used metrics with a clearly defined composite adverse-outcome gold standard (death, CRRT, MODS, or other severe complication); SHAP is a formally defined method (Lundberg & Lee) appropriately applied to the stated interpretability goal. QR_Faithfulness=2: 'coefficient of variation for SHAP values across 100 resampling iterations remaining below 15%, confirming the model's reliability in clinical application scenarios' -- an explicit explanation-stability metric, though this is stability across bootstrap-retrained models rather than fidelity of a single fixed model. QR_Reporting=1: underlying models and dataset (n=942, 5 Hainan hospitals, 2019-2021) are described in full replicable detail, but the SHAP configuration itself is never specified (no explainer variant named), a QR5 gap.
Notes: Clinical domain is Emergency Medicine/Toxicology rather than a clean fit to the controlled Domain vocabulary; coded EHR as the closest available category (2026-07-23 decision log: EHR/Other split kept as-is, no EmergencyMedicine value added). Single XAI method (SHAP) used throughout. Clinician_Design=Yes per the 2026-07-23 cross-paper consistency rule: authors are Emergency Medicine-affiliated and 'feature selection was based on clinical accessibility,' with rash 'retained in the simplified model to enhance clinical interpretability' -- clinician co-authorship plus clinically-motivated feature selection, matching the Xie_2021 pattern, even without a described formal co-design process. Trust_Claim=None per the 2026-07-23 cross-paper consistency rule: N_Participants=0, zero human engagement of any kind with the explanation; the paper's trust language ('allows physicians to understand and validate the model's reasoning process') is authorial rhetoric only, matching the Sulaiman_2025 pattern rather than Arnaud_2023/Juang_2026 (which had actual, if informal, human engagement).
Method_Justification_Notes: Introduction: 'Our SHAP-enhanced approach addresses the critical black box limitation of machine learning models in healthcare, providing clinicians with interpretable explanations for each prediction. This transparency is essential for clinical adoption and regulatory compliance, as it allows physicians to understand and validate the model's reasoning process.' Combines Cognitive grounds (comprehension/validation of reasoning) and Workflow grounds (clinical adoption, regulatory compliance) -- no explicit comparison to alternative XAI methods (LIME, Grad-CAM, etc.) explaining why SHAP specifically was chosen over them.
Reg_Notes: Reg_Comprehension=No: no comprehension check or correct-interpretation task administered to any clinician. Reg_TrustCalibration=No: Trust_Claim=None -- no trust measure or claim tied to any actual human engagement; the paper's trust language is authorial rhetoric only, with zero human participants (N_Participants=0). Reg_UncertaintyTransparency=No: the paper discusses a caveat that 'in cases of missing input features or low model confidence, clinicians should default to their professional expertise' but this is a stated limitation/recommendation, not a tested or implemented system feature surfacing uncertainty to the user; the deployed calculator outputs a bare risk probability with no confidence interval, OOD flag, or reliability caveat shown to the user. Reg_WorkflowSafety=No: cross-checks consistently -- Realism_Level=1 (<3) and EV_Environment=0 (<2); no realistic clinical workflow evaluation was conducted, only retrospective internal test-set validation.

Title: Emergency department narratives for early risk stratification of serious disposition in older adults after falls: A survival modelling study with external validation
Realism_Notes: Highest evaluation component achieved is proxy-metric only: aggregated LIME coefficients filtered by a computational signal-to-noise ratio (>=0.8) and sign-consistency threshold (>=0.6) across narratives, with no human participants at any stage. Meets the rubric's explicit 'common miscoding' case: real clinical data (NEISS ED narratives) with proxy metrics only and no human involvement is coded Level 1 even though the underlying data is real clinical text.
EV_Notes: All four EV dimensions score 0 because the LIME analysis is a purely computational cohort-level summary: no participants (EV_Participant=0), no elicited human decision task (EV_Task=0; 'aggregated LIME analysis performed on the development model to identify word-level drivers' is descriptive, not a task), no interface presented to any user (EV_Environment=0), and the outcome is the survival-model discrimination/calibration metrics plus the LIME stability filter, not a human-judged or patient outcome (EV_Outcome=0). Fully consistent with Realism_Level=1; no inconsistency to flag.
Outcome_Claimed: Abstract/Highlights: 'Aggregated LIME reveals distinct injury-driven vs. frailty-driven prognostic trajectories' and conclusion: 'Findings from aggregated LIME analyses suggest that survival modelling with large-capacity transformer embeddings could support early risk stratification, capturing a clinically important distinction between injury-driven and frailty-driven trajectories to serious dispositions that binary classifiers discard by design.'
Outcome_Demonstrated: Model discrimination: IPCW C-index 0.776 (development) and 0.724 (external validation), 'demonstrating discrimination above chance.' For the XAI component specifically: aggregated LIME word-coefficients retained only if they appear in >=1% of narratives, achieve signal-to-noise ratio >=0.8, and exhibit sign consistency >=0.6 across narratives (Section 3.6), yielding a stable cohort-level word list (e.g., 'nursing home', 'weak' -> low severity; 'slip', 'step', 'landing', 'found', 'unwitnessed' -> high severity) distinguishing an injury-driven from a frailty/context-driven trajectory (Section 5.4). This is a computational stability demonstration, not a human-validated or clinically-adjudicated interpretability finding.
QR_Notes: QR_Participant=2: no human participants, and claims are scoped to model/narrative-feature findings with explicit caveats ('Prospective validation on real-time triage notes is warranted'; NEISS narratives are 'abstracted 24-48 hours post-visit... real-time triage documentation will differ'). QR_Task=2: the aggregated-LIME analysis (Section 3.6) directly targets the stated aim 'to characterize the narrative features driving model predictions.' QR_Outcome=2: survival-discrimination metrics (IPCW C-index, td-AUC, IBS, BSS) are formally defined with citations (Appendix); the LIME aggregation/filtering procedure is explicit (SNR>=0.8, sign consistency>=0.6, frequency>=1%) and 'motivated by' Zafar & Khan's DLIME paper [38]. QR_Faithfulness=2: coded as Direct, consistent with the Han_2025 precedent (2026-07-23) -- the quality rubric's own worked example for QR4=2 explicitly lists 'stability metric (explanation consistency across similar inputs)'; the SNR/sign-consistency filter across all narratives is exactly this. QR_Reporting=2: XAI method, filtering thresholds, embedding models (with dimensionalities), XGBoost-AFT hyperparameter search, and dataset provenance/n are all fully specified with an Appendix.
Notes: Primary contribution is a retrospective/externally-validated survival model (XGBoost-AFT on NEISS ED fall narratives); LIME is a single, secondary, exploratory technique used only to interpret model behaviour at the cohort level -- not the paper's central object of study and not itself evaluated for fidelity/faithfulness beyond the stability filter. No clinician involvement anywhere in the paper: the only clinician mention is prospective/future 'co-design with emergency physicians and triage nurses' (Sections 5.6, 6), explicitly framed as necessary future work, not something conducted -- distinct from Xie_2021/Han_2025 since no clinician co-authors are on this paper and no clinically-motivated design input occurred, only a stated future intent. DOMAIN: this is an ED triage/disposition risk-stratification study but the controlled Domain vocabulary has no EmergencyMedicine value (2026-07-23 decision log: kept as Other, no schema change).
Method_Justification_Notes: No explicit statement of why LIME was chosen over alternative XAI methods (e.g., SHAP). The method section (3.6) states only 'we applied Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME)' with no comparative justification of computational, cognitive, or workflow grounds.
Reg_Notes: Reg_Comprehension=No: no comprehension test of any kind was administered to any human. Reg_TrustCalibration=No: no trust construct measured at all (Trust_Claim=None); the paper contains no clinician-facing trust element. Reg_UncertaintyTransparency=No: Brier Skill Score/calibration metrics quantify the survival model's own probability calibration for the researchers' internal evaluation, not uncertainty surfaced to an end-user via the explanation or interface -- no confidence scores or failure-mode flags are shown to any user. Reg_WorkflowSafety=No, consistent with Realism_Level=1 and EV_Environment=0: this is a fully retrospective, non-deployed analysis; paper explicitly defers workflow evaluation to future work ('Prospective validation on real-time triage notes is warranted,' Section 6).
